'Unbelievable' - Stephenson & Bellew react to Hrgovic's stoppage of Itauma
description: Shakur Stevenson and Tony Bellew believe Moses Itauma still has what it takes to become a world champion after losing to Filip Hrgovic for the IBF heavyweight title.
fullText:
Shakur Stevenson and Tony Bellew believe Moses Itauma showed enough in defeat by Filip Hrgovic to suggest he will become a heavyweight world champion.

Itauma made a fast start at London's O2 Arena and controlled large parts of the contest for the vacant IBF title, but eventually ran out of steam and was stopped by Hrgovic in round nine.

The Briton's speed and power caught the eye early in the bout but once he broke new ground - going beyond the sixth round for the first time in his career - the wheels began to come off.

Hrgovic was outpunched in every round until the decisive ninth when he seized his moment to become Croatia's first heavyweight world champion.

BBC Radio 5 Live's coverage of the night ended with Richie Woodhall, Ronald McIntosh and Steve Bunce offering up one word each to describe the night.

"Incredible," former super-middleweight world champion Woodhall said.

"Unbelievable," added commentator McIntosh, while Bunce signed off with "unforgettable".

Relive Hrgovic's dramatic stoppage win over Itauma to claim IBF heavyweight title

Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight

Many expected Itauma, who stepped into the ring with a perfect record of 14 wins as a professional, to be coronated as the next British heavyweight star - although Hrgovic was rightly touted as his biggest test to date.

Aged 21, Itauma was seeking to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion of all-time and Britain's second-youngest world champion.

But lack of experience against a seasoned Hrgovic proved Itauma's undoing.

Hype around Itauma has been building since winning his pro debut in just 23 seconds in January 2023.

A string of highlight knockouts - winning 12 of his previous 14 bouts inside six rounds - had propelled the Chatham fighter to world-title level in quick fashion.

Despite coming up short against 34-year-old Hrgovic, he is still being tipped to reach the pinnacle of boxing's glamour division.

"Unbelievable talent and skills," four-weight world champion Stevenson wrote on X.

"He's young and will be a champion one day if he learns from that. He throws every punch at 100mph and that can be a gift and a curse, Especially in the heavyweights division!"

Fellow Briton Tony Bellew, who was a cruiserweight world champion but ended his career at heavyweight, was also keen to focus on the positives.

"Moses Itauma will be world champion! He will learn so much from tonight," Bellew posted on X.

"The biggest thing I'll take from tonight is just how brave and tough Moses was, we knew Filip was super tough. Tonight we learned Moses is also tough, once he learns to pace a 12-round bout, he's gonna rule for a while! Filip Hrgovic's chin needs to studied."

Itauma told BBC Sport in the weeks before his heavyweight title fight that he had never even sparred 12 rounds, and it showed as he grew fatigued with each round that passed.

Trainer Ben Davison almost threw in the towel early in the ninth round as Itauma staggered around the ring, but he had second thoughts.

It was only moments later that the towel did come in as referee Howard Foster had stepped in to wave off the contest with Itauma unable to stand without the ropes to aid him.

Chris Eubank Jr wrote on X: "Not sure what happened tonight. Moses was fighting well and then gassed out it seems… at his young age this should simply not be happening. Time to rethink his training camp moving forward I think."

title: Heavyweight Itauma handed harsh world-title lesson
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma was taught a harsh lesson at world level - what can he learn from defeat and where does the 21-year-old go next?
fullText:
Moses Itauma was still a schoolboy when he would turn up at boxing gyms in his uniform and give seasoned professionals a hiding.

On Saturday night at the O2 Arena, the 21-year-old was finally given an education, as the Briton ran out of gas and the granite experience of Filip Hrgovic carried the Croatian to the vacant IBF heavyweight title.

The referee waved off the fight as Itauma's corner threw in the towel in the ninth round. But for long spells, Itauma was the quicker, sharper and more assured fighter, repeatedly finding Hrgovic with the left hand and showing exactly why so many inside boxing believe he has the tools to reach the very top.

Yet what made the contest so compelling was the growing sense that, even while Itauma was winning rounds, he was drifting closer to defeat.

'Unbelievable' - Stephenson, Bellew & others react to Hrgovic's stoppage of Itauma

Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London

His mouth opened in search of air and the spring disappeared from his legs. Hrgovic, hardened by the kind of difficult nights Itauma had never experienced, simply stayed there and waited for the younger man's body to betray him.

The sight afterwards was a sobering one as Itauma - who suffered a first defeat in his 15th pro fight - left the arena on a stretcher, before being taken to hospital.

"It's precautionary that he's gone to the hospital. That's what we always do to make sure because the most important thing is the boxer's health," promoter Frank Warren said.

"He's done something to his leg as well and he was quite tired. It was a high paced, fast fight for both the guys."

The remarkable night should not be remembered as the moment Itauma was exposed as incapable of operating at world level - his boxing showed the opposite.

What it exposed was the difference between possessing world-level talent and having the conditioning, experience and ring craft required to manage a 12-round world-title fight.

It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the build-up uncomfortable.

Hrgovic spent fight week repeatedly attacking Itauma's age, dismissing him as "just a kid". As the week wore on, Itauma looked increasingly irritated and eventually lost his composure at the weigh-in, shoving Hrgovic before the Croatian responded with a slap.

Itauma prides himself on being unusually cerebral for a heavyweight. He reads psychology and self-help books, talks openly about sharpening his mind and appears to spend far more time analysing himself than most 21-year-olds.

But there is always a danger that deep thinking becomes overthinking, something Anthony Joshua has been accused of repeatedly during the latter stages of his career.

Whether the pre-fight barbs played any part or not, Itauma's gameplan once the bell rang was clear; he wanted to end the night early.

"Someone said to me he doesn't feel like he'd win a world title unless he knocks him out. I didn't like that," Warren said.

That mindset was understandable because it had served Itauma extraordinarily well until now. But perhaps Hrgovic had been underestimated by almost everybody - Itauma, the media, pundits, former fighters and bookmakers who installed the Briton as a heavy favourite.

Hrgovic is an Olympic bronze medallist who went 12 hard rounds with the giant Zhilei Zhang, while against Daniel Dubois - the only defeat on his record - he was leading on two of the three scorecards before the fight was stopped because of cuts.

'El Animal' knew what it felt like to be hurt, to become tired and to remain in a fight when things were going badly. Itauma did not.

The eighth round summed up both Itauma's extraordinary talent and his lack of experience. He threw more punches than in any other round of the fight, pouring what remained of his energy into trying to remove a man who had already demonstrated that he was exceptionally difficult to remove.

"He was throwing too much. He was fighting like an amateur," Hrgovic said afterwards. "I knew I needed to endure it. I need to stay there. He will get tired and I'll get him in the later rounds."

There are questions about the Chatham fighter's preparation, too. Itauma - who had never gone beyond six rounds professionally - admitted before the fight that he had never even sparred 12 rounds.

His conditioning was clearly not where it needed to be for a championship fight and responsibility for that cannot rest solely with the fighter - it also falls on the experienced team entrusted with preparing him.

Itauma showed that many of the qualities which looked spectacular against lesser opposition still worked against a genuine world-level heavyweight.

He proved he can take a punch - there was no single blow that suddenly revealed a fragile chin. His hand speed troubled Hrgovic and he made the Zagreb fighter look slow.

So with those positives in mind, where does he go from here?

"Don't give up. Don't lose confidence. Get a few easy fights, easy wins. Build again and learn off these mistakes. You can't box like an amateur. It's a 12-round fight, you need to pace yourself," was Hrgovic's advice.

Warren remains convinced that Itauma is one of the most exceptional talents he has encountered, pointing towards two-time world champion Dubois as a prime example of a heavyweight who rebuilt successfully after painful setbacks.

But British boxing has seen the other side of that story too, of course - where fighters like David Price were once regarded as the country's next great heavyweight hope before successive defeats damaged an aura they never fully recovered.

Audiences will now scrutinise Itauma's every move, his breathing and how he paces a fight. That vulnerability may actually make him a more compelling fighter to follow.

The aura of untouchable perfection is gone. The schoolboy has been taught a lesson and now we will find out what he learns from it.

title: Faster, higher, funnier: what we learned from China’s robot games
description:
Five-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rear
With exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief.

The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ran quicker than Usain Bolt before slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.

fullText:
With exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief.

The five-day showcase staked out China’s claim to undisputed leadership in humanoid robotics as android martial artists landed knockout roundhouse kicks and robot teams marched into the arena heralded by flag-waving captains astride giant robotic dogs. The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ran quicker than Usain Bolt before slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.

There, in a 10-second clip perfect for the games’ global online audience, was proof of what onlooking international experts described as the superpower’s “staggering” engineering progress, combined with comfort that the disintegrating robots might not yet be ready to become humanity’s overlords.

“Ready for another big day of fail,” read a typically schadenfreude-laced comment from one of millions who tuned into viral social media clips and livestreams of events from boxing to breakdancing in which the humanoids displayed a jerky mix of ruthless effectiveness and pathetic failure.

Others caught themselves experiencing unexpected empathy. One captioned a robot struggling through the 400m obstacle race: “after drinking 4 bottles of wine at 2 a.m”. Another found a weightlifting contest “way more emotional than I expected” as the bots strained to achieve their sporting goals.

If the games had a slogan it might be: faster, higher, funnier. The obstacle course involving humanoids scrambling under nets, down stairs and over stepping stones reminded the comedian Charlie Higson of Monty Python’s Upper Class Twit of the Year sketch: “It’s only lacking ‘taking the bra off the debs’ and ‘shooting themselves’.” He came back the next day for more. “They get better and better,” he tweeted as a cheerleader robot wielding glittery pom-poms flailed around like it was having a fit.

But the games were not intended to only entertain. Involving over 2,000 humanoids built by more than 660 mostly domestic tech companies, it was a propaganda flex of China’s robotics muscle just weeks before its president, Xi Jinping, lands in Washington DC for a summit with Donald Trump, where the superpowers’ race to tech supremacy will be high on the agenda. Only last month Trump banned imports of Chinese humanoids and four-legged robot dogs, citing cyber and national security concerns. The event was also a billboard to boost global sales of Chinese robots as US rivals prepare their own launches, notably Elon Musk’s long-hyped Optimus humanoid which is reported to have finally gone into production this month. Last year China produced 12,800 humanoids, about 90% of the global total, according to the Mercator Institute for Chinese Studies, a dominance which perhaps gave China the confidence to candidly broadcast so many comic failures, which surprised some onlookers.

The event reflected the fact that, for the Chinese Communist party, humanoids are a high priority, offering solutions to a looming demographic crunch in the labour market, rising military ambitions and, as they walk more widely among the people, the state’s desire to tighten its surveillance web. Beijing is fuelling an intensely competitive robot industry by seeding hundreds of companies to create an evolutionary survival of the fittest dynamic, with the games creating a hard deadline for competitors to deliver measurable progress. Xi’s latest five-year plan, approved in March, was studded with pledges to boost robotics industries; accelerate the “practical application of … humanoid robots” and explore “embodied AI in roles experiencing labour shortages or high-risk environments” which likely include war. The military potential of the humanoids on display worried some onlookers.

“Fascinating, and honestly, a little scary,” said Arun Bothra, a senior police officer in India, which shares a tense border with China. “Watching robots run, play football and compete like humans is one thing. Seeing them on borders someday, carrying guns and making decisions, will be something else entirely.” Or as another viewer concluded while watching a humanoid hoist a loaded barbell in the weightlifting contest: “Humanity is preparing its own end”.

Of course China is not alone in pursuing robotic warfare. As the Beijing games progressed on Monday, Ukraine was staging a novel military parade in Kyiv made up entirely of robotic weaponry and defence equipment.

But how to explain the numerous crashes and fits in the Olympic speed skating arena where the competition took place? Experts said the games revealed how China was making the most rapid strides in developing humanoids’ bodies rather than their minds.

“The progress they have made from last year is staggering,” said Thrishantha Nanayakkara, a professor of robotics at the Dyson school of design engineering at Imperial College London. “Everything seems to be coming together …. by 2030, it will be a very different world.”

The fastest sprinter, Tiangong Ultra, completed the 100m more than twice as fast as last year, while the peak standing jump rose from 0.96 m to 3.40m. Liquid cooling has allowed Chinese engineers to increase the torque of the motors that drive their limbs creating more twitchy and powerful force.

“This execution is incredible,” said Ingo Keller, head of robotics at the National Robotarium, based at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh. “You would not have expected the speed of development. [But] does it move the goalpost in utilising humanoids? Not necessarily.”

Experts stress the games revealed progress in specialist, not generalist, humanoids: the robots were fast runners or good boxers, not both, partly because the AI models that govern their decisions are yet to be able to process the physical world’s full complexity. The industry talks about reaching a ChatGPT moment – a tipping point when humanoid technology becomes generally useful and explodes into the mainstream. By one definition, that comes when a robot can succeed at 80% of tasks in an unfamiliar home, instructed by voice or text. The event coincided with a sobering speech from Wang Xingxing, founder of Unitree, one of China’s leading robotics companies, who said it could be a decade before that ChatGPT moment.

“Humanoids are not yet capable enough for mass deployment,” he said. “The limitations in the AI models that power robots’ decision-making and interactions remain the industry’s biggest bottleneck.” Amid uncertainty about the impact of robotics and bubble fears, his company’s share price has been oscillating wildly since it listed in Shanghai earlier this month.

Georg Stieler, a consultant who advises multinational companies on robots, said he did not see much progress on robots’ autonomy when he was in Beijing this week. He reported that some Chinese robotics companies were also privately cynical about the five-day showcase, complaining about a lack of funding for commercial long-term pilot projects “to do something useful in a factory”.

“It’s not so difficult to make a stunt, which people will share on LinkedIn or X,” Stieler said. “The major challenge is to do something that’s really useful.”

Humanoid robot dexterity requires much more work and there was little focus on the events testing it. There was little obvious coverage of a Monty Pythonesque category that included power tool assembly, powder weighing, bottle opening, cap prying, box unpacking and tweezer bean-picking. One such challenge was briefly featured on Wednesday when the race track was occupied by the unspectacular sight of a humanoid struggling to pick up a small object from a table and spilling water in a pouring challenge. The cameras panned away to find a humanoid martial artist carving the air with kicks.

title: Cacace to face Ball in Belfast world title defence
description: Anthony Cacace will make the first defence of his WBA super-featherweight world title against Nick Ball at The 02 in Belfast on 19 December.
fullText:
Anthony Cacace will make the first defence of his WBA super-featherweight world title against Nick Ball at The 02 in Belfast on 19 December.

The 37-year-old from Belfast won the title in March with a points victory of James 'Jazza' Dickens in Dublin and will face another Liverpool native in former featherweight champion Ball.

Cacace's last fight in his home city occurred in May 2023 with a defence of the IBO belt against Damian Wrzesinski on the undercard of Luis Alberto Lopez's featherweight title victory over Michael Conlan.

Since then, he has won and then relinquished the IBF title before becoming a two-time champion at the weight with victory over Dickens which saw his record improve to 25 wins with one loss.

"Nick's a great fighter, ex-world champion, so I expect a good scrap. He's a hard man, so let's do it," Cacace told DAZN.

"I'll fight with him, I'll box him - whatever way he wants, so we'll see what happens on the night. I'm really looking forward to it.

"Belfast around Christmas time is going to be jumping, so I'm looking forward to it."

Ball is coming off his first career defeat when stopped in the final round by Brandon Figueroa in a defence of the WBA featherweight title in February.

The Liverpudlian won the title in 2024 with a points verdict over Raymond Ford, three months after his first bid for world honours ended in a draw against then-WBC champion Rey Vargas.

He fought on the same Belfast card as Cacace in 2023 when stopping Ludumo Lamati, who suffered a stroke in the ring but has since recovered, and is relishing the chance to become a two-weight champion.

"It's a massive opportunity at a new weight," said Ball, whose record is 23-1-1.

"He's a solid champion, so it's going to be a good fight. I'll be coming, he'll be coming, so it's going to be a good one."

title: Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London
description: Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO heavyweight world title against the man he dethroned Fabio Wardley in a rematch on 17 October in London.
fullText:
Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO heavyweight world title against former champion Fabio Wardley in a highly anticipated rematch on 17 October at London's O2 Arena.

Londoner Dubois, 28, dethroned Wardley with an 11th-round stoppage in a thrilling all-British showdown in Manchester in May to become a two-time world champion.

It was announced during Saturday's undercard of Moses Itauma's IBF heavyweight world title fight with Filip Hrgovic, with Dubois and Wardley facing off in the ring.

Dubois said he is predicting a "dominant victory" before adding: "Let's get it on. It's just a war.

"When you get in the water, you're going to get wet. We will see. Give me some of that face-to-face - boy."

The first meeting lived up to its billing, with two of the division's biggest punchers producing a dramatic fight that showcased the power of both men.

Wardley dropped Dubois twice early in the contest, but a bloodied Wardley absorbed heavy punishment before the referee stopped the bout.

It was the first defeat of the 31-year-old's professional career in his 22nd bout.

"It didn't take long at all [to agree]. The O2 is like a home away from home for me," Fabio Wardley said on DAZN.

"Looking forward to getting straight back into it. Going to be a rematch and going to be revenge.

"We came into the fight with all the confidence in the world, but adjustments needed to be made."

The Ipswich fighter's rise through the sport has been remarkable. Having only taken up boxing at the age of 19, he progressed through the unlicensed white-collar scene before reaching the top of the heavyweight division.

Dubois, meanwhile, has experienced the full spectrum of boxing's highs and lows.

The 26-fight veteran has suffered three defeats during his career but rebuilt himself to claim world honours twice, with his victory over Wardley marking the latest chapter in his comeback story.

The winner of the rematch could be in line for a blockbuster fight next summer against fellow Briton Itauma, provided the heavyweight prospect secures a world title of his own.

The winner of the contest between Itauma and Hrgovic will be required to face mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez.

Should Itauma - who is aiming to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion in history after Mike Tyson - come through both fights, promoter Frank Warren has suggested a potential Wembley Stadium clash with the winner of Dubois-Wardley II next summer.

title: Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight
description: Filip Hrgovic shatters Moses Itauma's world-title dream as the Briton appears to punch himself out in an extraordinary heavyweight world-title contest in London.
fullText:
Filip Hrgovic ripped up the script and shattered Moses Itauma's world-title dream as the Briton appeared to punch himself out in an extraordinary heavyweight contest in London.

Itauma, 21, controlled most of the fight and scored a second-round knockdown but faded as his relentless output caught up with him.

Hrgovic weathered the storm and piled on the pressure in the ninth. With Itauma barely able to stand, his legs unsteady and body swaying before slumping in the corner, his team threw in the towel.

Itauma - who needed medical attention before leaving the arena on a stretcher - had been a heavy favourite after tearing through his first 14 opponents and was spoken about as heavyweight boxing's next superstar.

"He is the best I have been in the ring with, but he needs more experience. I knew I was losing the round, but I knew that I had the pace in my favour. He needs more experience, but he is one of a kind," Hrgovic said.

"From the first round, I saw his gassing out. He started fast. I knew he was going to gas out. I knew when my chance came I needed to push. That is what I did."

With the vacant IBF title on the line, victory would have made Itauma the second-youngest world champion in the division's history.

Instead, his inexperience began to show as his Croatian opponent - an Olympic bronze medallist whose only previous professional defeat came against Daniel Dubois - survived everything Itauma threw at him before completing a remarkable turnaround.

Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London

Cameron beats Mayer to become unified light-middleweight champion

Hrgovic - wearing the red and white checks of his country - made his entrance first to a wall of boos, before the mood inside the O2 Arena flipped as Itauma emerged to a huge roar - taking his time and soaking up the reception.

The crowd had made its allegiances clear after a fiery build-up which included Itauma shoving Hrgovic, the Zagreb man slapping him back and plenty of verbal sparring.

Itauma came out with real intent, landing straight lefts from his southpaw stance. Hrgovic is known for his durability but struggled to keep pace with the Briton's speed early on.

Early in the second, a right hook knocked Hrgovic off-balance and his glove touched the canvas. Oasis star Noel Gallagher and boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed were among those watching as the crowd gasped at almost every Itauma punch, whether it landed or not.

But by the end of the third, Itauma - who had boxed just 26 professional rounds before his first world-title fight - was already breathing heavily.

There had also been questions over his chin, simply because it had never really been tested. Hrgovic began landing the occasional heavy shot but Itauma took them well and fired straight back.

A fight in the crowd momentarily took attention away from the action in the fifth before an Itauma uppercut in the closing seconds brought the focus back to the ring.

Itauma continued to fire combinations but Hrgovic was barely budging. A huge right landed on the bell in the sixth and another followed in the seventh, yet the Croatian simply walked through them.

The Briton was well ahead but, rather than box his way towards victory, he continued to chase the knockout. A flurry in the eighth backed Hrgovic on to the ropes and had him in trouble, but Itauma was grimacing between exchanges and looking increasingly spent.

The youngster somehow stayed upright but his legs had gone. Hrgovic continued to press and when Itauma slumped into his corner, exhausted and barely able to defend himself, referee Howard Foster waved off the contest as the towel came in.

Hrgovic admitted he had been "outboxed" but leaves London as Croatia's first heavyweight world champion, with Frank Sanchez waiting as the IBF mandatory challenger.

A unification fight could follow, with Daniel Dubois holding the WBO title and set to face Fabio Wardley again in October.

For Itauma, this was supposed to be a coronation.

Instead, he leaves the O2 Arena with questions over whether the step up came too soon.

He has time to rebuild and there will be a strong feeling that, with a little more experience, this night could have ended very differently.

Londoner Dubois was stopped by Joe Joyce as an unbeaten 23-year-old before going on to become a two-time world champion. Itauma has even more time on his side.

"He's an amazing fighter," Hrgovic said. "I am the present. He is definitely the future."

Promoter Frank Warren suggested Itauma was carrying a leg injury in the final round but backed him to return.

"Moses gave everything," he added. "He has to go back to the drawing board and he can come again."

The expectation around Itauma will not disappear entirely overnight but the aura of invincibility has gone.

Yadong's knockout surprise was stunning in more than one way. First, the actual knockout itself was incredible. Song timed a perfectly-placed right uppercut as Nurmagomedov dipped his head to the left during a level change. The fact that Nurmagomedov dropped like a sack of potatoes made the finish even more spectacular.

Adding to the fight itself were the betting odds associated with the UFC Shanghai main event. Yadong was not expected to win this weekend against a fighter in Nurmagomedov who many consider to be championship level. Fans haven't seen Song take that step up in his career yet so there was some hesitation to trust he could get it done. Needless to say, Yadong spoiled a lot of betting slips early Saturday as he flipped the script on Nurmagomedov's anticipated victory.

On top of that, Yadong was fighting on his home soil in China. Yadong fought in Macau this past May as well, but before that he hadn't competed at home since all the way back in 2018. Chinese fight fans had another chance to see Song perform and they made sure it counted. The atmosphere was absolutely electric, which created an unforgettable scene after Yadong finished Nurmagomedov.

The MMA community was left in shock and awe as they had witnessed one of the biggest upsets of the year and one of the biggest upsets in recent UFC bantamweight history. Some of the biggest names in the sport, including former UFC champions Sean O'Malley, Aljamain Sterling, Belal Muhammad, Merab Dvalishvili and Daniel Cormier, took to social media to share their reactions. title: AI and the Commons
description: As a global leader in open licensing and copyright, we have long stood at the intersection of innovation in the public interest, creativity, and access to knowledge. With the rise of consumer-facing generative AI, which is changing the way people share and access knowledge online, it became clear: CC had to act—urgently, but with care.…
fullText:
As a global leader in open licensing and copyright, we have long stood at the intersection of innovation in the public interest, creativity, and access to knowledge. With the rise of consumer-facing generative AI, which is changing the way people share and access knowledge online, it became clear: CC had to act—urgently, but with care.

In response, we launched a global consultation effort. We hosted workshops in New York, Boston, San Francisco, London, and Berlin. We attended conferences and convenings globally and tracked and engaged in the development of AI policy and legislation.

A clear message emerged: many creators and communities feel uneasy about their content being used to develop AI without transparency and are seeking ways to regain agency. Our community has called on us to intervene with new tools that help rebalance power, ultimately infusing the AI ecosystem with reciprocity.

This moment mirrors another inflection point: the rise of the mainstream internet in the early 2000s. Back then, CC challenged the “all rights reserved” vs. “no rights reserved” binary by offering nuanced, practical tools for creators. The CC licenses made it easy to share and have been applied to tens of billions of works on the internet, growing the creative commons and increasing access to knowledge.

Today’s AI challenges call for similarly creative but practical solutions. Once again, sharing on the internet is being tested. Once again, the commons is at stake.

CC is striving to make sure that AI doesn’t lead to a more closed internet or reduce public access to knowledge and culture.

Once again, Creative Commons is challenging the all-or-nothing binary to offer another way.

The AI landscape is complex. Our principled response to sharing in the age of AI is simple.

AI is built on the commons. To serve the public interest, AI must help grow, not diminish, the commons, ensuring benefits are widely shared. We need a new social contract, anchored in reciprocity and a shared commitment to the commons. Here is our plan.

Open access through CC licenses created a spectrum of sharing. Today we need something similar for AI: a spectrum of participation, where creators and data-holding stewards are active participants in how knowledge is produced, shared, and used. CC is advancing several high-impact interventions as part of the CC signals framework to restore trust, strengthen participation, and embed public interest values into the AI knowledge ecosystem.

While CC signals are designed to directly address the challenges raised by AI, CC licenses and public domain tools still have an important role to play. We are continually monitoring and helping to make sense of the complex relationship between AI, copyright, and the CC licenses.

👉 

We advocate for AI policies that protect the public interest and uphold the values of access to knowledge. We work with policy makers and other civil society organizations to ensure AI policy advances the public interest.

This is a shared challenge, and a shared opportunity.

Whether you’re a funder, developer, policymaker, educator, platform operator, or creator, your participation matters.

title: U.S. takes out refueling station for alleged drug-trafficking boats
description: The vessel, which was in international waters near Ecuador, was allegedly used as a floating refueling station for drug boats belonging to the Los Choneros organization.
fullText:
The U.S. military, in conjunction with Ecuadorian officials, boarded and later sank a vessel on Friday allegedly used as a refueling station for drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean, according to U.S. Southern Command.

The vessel, which was in international waters near Ecuador, was allegedly used as a floating ship-to-ship refueling station for drug boats belonging to the Los Choneros organization.

The ship was boarded by Marines and sailors from the USS San Antonio and cleared without incident, SOCOM said. The people taken off the boat were then taken to Ecuador, and the U.S. sank the boat with an airstrike, SOCOM said, which also provided video of the ship being scuttled.

"Today's operation is a stark example of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition's power to dismantle the sophisticated, clandestine narco-terrorist tactics and capabilities that have enabled the trafficking of dangerous drugs destined for American communities," SOCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said in a statement. "Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region. Together with our regional partners, we are committed to defeating narco-terrorists in the Western Hemisphere."

"Today's interdiction and sinking of a floating refueling station used for at-sea drug trafficking operations dealt a direct blow to the logistics network fueling narco-terrorists and cartels in the Western Hemisphere.

— U.S. Southern Command (@Southcom) August 29, 2026

The strike comes as the U.S. continues to target alleged drug traffickers with deadly strikes on small boats in the eastern Pacific and Caribbean. The latest strike came on Tuesday when four people were killed in a boat strike in the Caribbean.

That attack brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" almost a year ago.

The last strike on an alleged drug boat in the Pacific Ocean came on Sunday, when two people were killed. It was the first strike after a pause of more than two months in the U.S. campaign against alleged smugglers.

Ecuadorian officials have been battling the Los Choneros gang for years. The drug-trafficking organization, named for the city of Chone in western Ecuador, was led for years by José Adolfo Macías Villamar.

Macías escaped from jail in 2024 while serving a 34-year sentence for drug trafficking, after which a large-scale gang war broke out on the streets of the capital of Quito. The gang wars expanded to Guayaquil and the nearby town of Nobol. Gunmen even stormed a studio in Guayaquil and fired off shots on live TV. New President Daniel Noboa was forced to call in the army to quell the violence.

Macías, who was indicted by the U.S. Department of Justice on drug and weapons charges in April 2025, was recaptured two months later and extradited to the U.S. in July 2025. He pleaded not guilty to charges that he imported thousands of pounds of cocaine into the United States. He is still awaiting trial.

title: Henshaw wins world gold 11 days after being in hospital
description: Britain's Charlotte Henshaw has won her 12th Para-canoe World Championship title - less than two weeks after being in hospital with cellulitis.
fullText:
Britain's Charlotte Henshaw has won her 12th Para-canoe World Championship title - less than two weeks after being in hospital with cellulitis.

The 39-year-old contracted the condition - usually a bacterial infection which makes the skin painful, hot and swollen - in her leg and, after leaving hospital, was unable to train on the water in the lead up to the championships in Poznan, Poland.

But in Saturday's KL2 200m final she crossed the finish line more than three seconds ahead of the rest of the field for her eighth world title in the event, adding to the four she has won in the VL3 equivalent.

"Of all the titles I've managed to win, that probably means the most because I did not know I was going to be here a week ago," she said.

"There's maybe something to be said for taking the pressure off and going out and trusting my body and my experience.

"I've been competing at the highest level for an awfully long time and in moments where things aren't going well and the preparation gets swept out from underneath you, you have to draw on every single bit of experience.

"Eleven days ago, I didn't think I would be on the plane so to come here and compete and then retain my title, I couldn't be happier and it means a lot this one."

A double leg amputee, Henshaw is a three-time Paralympic champion in Para-canoeing since switching from swimming in 2017.

Writing on Instagram, external after her heat on Friday, Henshaw said: "The last week or so has definitely put things into perspective.

"It's so easy to get caught up in results, rankings, times and expectations, but when your long-term limb health becomes the priority, those things seem a lot less important."

Elsewhere in Poznan on Saturday, Henshaw's team-mate Hope Gordon won gold in the KL3 200m while Stuart Wood won bronze in the men's VL3 event.

For Gordon, who last month represented Scotland in Para-powerlifting at the Commonwealth Games, it is a first KL3 world title - having previously won two in the VL3.

title: South Africa hold off All Blacks fightback to level series
description: World champions South Africa deliver a powerful first-half performance as they edge past New Zealand and level 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1.
fullText:
'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second Test

Tries: Kriel, De Allende, Kolisi Cons: Kolbe 3 Pens: Kolbe 4

Tries: Roigard, McKenzie, Carter, Savea Cons: Love 3

World champions South Africa delivered a powerful first-half performance as they edged past New Zealand and levelled 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1 with two Tests to play.

The All Blacks travelled to Cape Town knowing a win would write them into the history books as the first New Zealand team to win back-to-back Tests in South Africa since the 'Incomparables' of 1996.

But South Africa dominated the basics and showed a more clinical edge this week, even though the lively All Blacks again outscored them on the try count by four to three.

New Zealand's fightback ultimately came too late, captain Ardie Savea barging over on 77 minutes to get the game within a score, but on the All Blacks' final attack Boks replacement Cameron Hanekom won a superb turnover that settled the nervy closing stages.

As he did last week, Springboks wing Cheslin Kolbe took on the kicking duties over fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, notching up 18 points in a player-of-the-match performance.

The first series in 30 years between these two mighty rugby nations is shaping into an epic, with the third Test back at altitude in Soweto, Johannesburg next Saturday.

The Springbok team that took the field at the Cape Town Stadium was markedly different to the one originally named by head coach Rassie Erasmus on Monday.

Fly-half Handre Pollard was fit and then injured and withdrawn in the week, while Kolbe was injured and then fit and eventually named on the wing.

On top of that, Erasmus switched around his whole front row in the hours before kick-off, with the starting trio dropping to the bench and vice-versa.

It meant there were five changes in all from the matchday squad announced on Monday and surely would have had the New Zealand management thumbing through the regulations of the tour agreement.

Despite producing a famous rearguard effort in the first-Test victory at Ellis Park, New Zealand boss Dave Rennie warned in the week his side would need to "go deeper" to cope with the inevitable Springbok backlash.

That South African onslaught came from the off.

Hooker Deon Fourie, at nearly 40 the oldest Springbok in history, found his target in the line-out, the South African maul powered into the 22, and lightning fast ball led to centre Jesse Kriel crashing over.

Kolbe added the extras as the world champions made the dream start.

But despite the fast start from the hosts, New Zealand grew into the contest, with referee Angus Gardner, himself a late call-up in place of Nika Amashukeli, presiding over a fast and fluent game.

Damian McKenzie made a clean break which almost put in Will Jordan, and while the Boks killed the ball from the ensuing breakdown, Eben Etzebeth got up to spoil New Zealand's five-metre line-out.

Despite their set-piece issues, the All Blacks came again. Intricate handling freed Jordan, who used his pace and strength to escape down the right and link with the outstanding Cam Roigard. Ruben Love levelled the scores from bang in front.

That score lit a fire in the Springboks, with Kolbe kicking a penalty and Damian de Allende barrelling over after another imposing maul as South Africa showed far more ruthlessness compared to a week ago.

With the Springboks dominating in the basics, the crowd in Cape Town smelt blood as the lead stretched to 17-7.

But with ball in hand, Rennie's crop are reminiscent of the great All Blacks side of old. Savea burst forward from a line-out, and perfect passing gave McKenzie a walk-in.

At 17-14 edging towards half-time the contest was in the balance, before a match-defining sequence just before the interval.

Kolbe forced a five-metre scrum, before which Erasmus brought on two of his strongest scrummagers in Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche, who immediately won a penalty.

From there, another scrum, another penalty advantage, and with the All Blacks back-pedalling captain Siya Kolisi crashed over for South Africa's third try and a 10-point lead after a pulsating first 40.

New Zealand needed to score first in the second half, and they didn't, losing the ball when in Bok territory and then giving away a soft penalty which Kolbe kicked.

The All Blacks were on the ropes, Marx won a breakdown penalty, and Kolbe stretched the lead to 16 points with half an hour to go.

With the second half lacking the fireworks of the first, the All Blacks backs – led by Roigard - desperately tried to drag New Zealand back into the match.

After another McKenzie break led to nothing, some more beautiful handling resulted in Leroy Carter scampering into the left corner, a fabulous finish.

More excellent attacking play released Jordan down the right, and the recycled ball found skipper Savea, who crashed over to cut the gap to seven points with two minutes remaining.

But the Springboks held on, despite lock Lood de Jager being sent to the sin-bin for a high tackle.

Fittingly, it was a breakdown penalty that settled the game, with Hanekom winning the crucial turnover in an area South Africa dominated.

The All Blacks' impressive win in the first Test had temporarily shot them above South Africa in the world rankings, something Erasmus urged his side to rectify.

That they did, and with normal service resumed in the eyes of the Springboks supporters, South Africa travel back to the Highveld with the momentum.

But the All Blacks have played some wonderful rugby in the first two Tests, and will still believe they can join the legends of 1996.

The eyes of the rugby world now turn to Soweto.

Florida native Ross Chastain calls Daytona Cup pole a "life achievement"
description: Chastain grew up less than two hours away from Daytona International Speedway
fullText:
Ross Chastain has never been known for his qualifying performances. In fact, he became the only driver to ever win the Coca-Cola 600 from last place on the grid in 2025.

But Friday at Daytona, he rocketed to the top of the charts, taking pole position by half-a-tenth over Chris Buescher.

It's just Chastain's third career pole in the NASCAR Cup Series, with his other two P1s coming at Watkins Glen in 2024 and Nashville in 2023 (a race he won).

"Yeah, it's almost indescribable," Chastain said of the pole in a post-qualifying press conference. "I think I should probably start with, like, I grasp that it doesn't have much bearing on knowing what tomorrow is going to bring, but for tonight and today for a new package, for Trackhouse to go and pick the right things for car build to come here and to execute through two rounds, it's incredible. We've been good in one round before, but not the second. So, yeah, it's very important to note that we chose the right things as a team to come here and execute through qualifying.

"I'll start this with -- I do not know what that means for tomorrow. I'm being honest, I have no idea what it means for tomorrow."

Of course, as Chastain notes, qualifying means very little a superspeedway. Last year, Ryan Blaney won the race from P1, but qualifying was rained out. The last true Daytona pole-sitter to win the race was Dale Earnhardt Jr. in the summer of 2015.

But besides that, it's still a very special moment for the Florida driver.

"Life achievement," said Chastain. "I was a kid sitting in the grandstands. We camped outside of turn one, gate 40. For those that remember back in, I don't know, late 90s, 2000s, early 2000s, it was not the nice, beautiful gate 40 with dry grass that you see now. It was a mud pit. We camped over there, rode our bikes around and had other families that were family and some that were more than family that were such close friends and my buddies that I grew up with.

"So, yeah, I mean, from the race pools, like getting the race day paper and drawing names out that they would cut up and hoping you got the pole-sitter, that was a big deal. And as I got older, I realized how much little or just less it means, as far as how the car is going to draft. But, still, it's a big deal. It's a life achievement that I will never forget. This is a moment I'll never forget."

It was also a great day for Trackhouse as an organization, with Chastain's teammates Shane van Gisbergen and Connor Zilisch qualifying sixth and seventh, respectively.

SVG is trying to hold onto the 16th and final spot inside the Chase field, and Chastain is fully aware of the role he may play in that battle.

"When there's an opportunity of two cars in front of me, I think everybody in the field knows that I'll push the 97 [SVG]," said Chastain. "I am OEM loyal and specifically 97 loyal. So when there's opportunity, any momentum I have, any push I have, will go to the 97. The crew chiefs will be talking. You know, there's little differences, and if we find something air pressure wise or something, the 97 will be the first to know."

However, Chastain surely wants to win too, as he is facing a winless streak that dates back to Memorial Day Weekend, 2025. Daytona will mark 49 races since his last trip to Cup Series Victory Lane, and the driver of the No. 1 has also managed to win at least one race in every year of the Next Gen era (since 2022).

title: NEW UFC Bantamweight Rankings After Song Shockingly Smashes Nurmagomedov at UFC Shanghai

fullText:
In the early morning hours in the United States, the MMA world leader returned to Paramount+ for UFC Shanghai. The card in China was headlined by a major matchup at bantamweight when rankings regular and native son, Yadong Song, took on top-five fighter Umar Nurmagomedov.

Despite the former title challenger being a solid favorite heading into the bout, the "Kung Fu Kid" scored a huge knockout victory in Round 2. Following the win, let's take a look at the updated UFC bantamweight rankings and where Song lands.

Marlon Vera has been one of the division's most entertaining fighters over the last six years. However, while he did eventually get himself a title opportunity, he has gone into a steep decline since trying to take the top spot at the mountaintop.

The fan-favorite Ecuadorian has lost four straight, with his latest coming in February as he came up just short in a clash with David Martinez in Mexico City. "Chito's" days as a top-10 fighter seem to be numbered.

After a pair of losses, Aiemann Zahabi was probably one more loss away from having to look for a job elsewhere. However, over the last five years, he has won seven straight, including a huge UFC 315 win over living legend Jose Aldo, then in his native Canada over Marlon Vera.

He got the biggest opportunity of his career at UFC Freedom 250 when he took on former champion Sean O'Malley. Unfortunately for him, he was outclassed and knocked out in Round 2. The loss probably ends the 38-year-old's hopes of ever fighting for UFC gold.

Cory Sandhagen has been many fight fans' favorite bantamweight for several years. He is gutsy, highly skilled, and rarely in a boring fight. In October 2025, he finally got an elusive title opportunity at UFC 320. Unfortunately, despite his best efforts, he was just another victim of former bantamweight king Merab Dvalishvili.

Sandhagen was back in the Octagon at UFC 329 but was outworked by rising star Mario Bautista. He has now lost three of his last four and is as far outside the title picture as he has ever been.

Umar Nurmagomedov has been one of the best bantamweights in the world for quite some time. In 2025, he had the chance to be the second Nurmagomedov to win gold in the UFC, but came up just short in a highly competitive clash with champion Merab Dvalishvili.

Following the defeat, he scored a pair of important decision wins over ranked fighters, Mario Bautista and Deiveson Figueiredo. However, with a possible title opportunity on the line, the Russian was shockingly KO'd by top-10 stalwart Song Yadong at UFC Shanghai in August. Ending any hope of a championship fight in 2026.

Yadong Song has long been seen as a fighter with the potential to fight for gold in the UFC one day. However, after putting a few wins together, he always seems to be halted by a key loss to one or two of the division's elites. That happened over the last couple of years when he lost matchups against former champions Sean O'Malley and Petr Yan.

However, following his loss to the American earlier this year, the Chinese star has rebounded with big wins. First, a submission victory over former flyweight champ Deiveson Figueiredo in May. Then at UFC Shanghai a few months later, he scored a nasty KO win over former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov. Thrusting him back into the contender conversation.

After an outstanding run in Combate Global, where he went 10-1, David Martinez has emerged as a top 10 bantamweight in the No. 1 company in the world, the UFC. After earning a contract on Dana White's Contender Series in 2024, he has reeled off three straight wins in the Octagon. Including a big victory over Marlon Vera in February. He has fairly earned his spot in our rankings after winning 10 straight overall.

Since his UFC debut seven years ago, Mario Bautista has steadily climbed the rankings. Scoring wins over top 15 talent like Jose Aldo and Ricky Simon. However, the biggest win of his career came at UFC 329 when he got a chance at revenge against Cory Sandhagen. The man who beat him in his UFC debut.

After three hard-fought rounds, the MMA Lab product earned a decision win and is right on the cusp of a title opportunity in the next year.

Former champ Sean O'Malley is one of the UFC's most popular fighters. He has the unique look, charisma, and most importantly, the knockout striking that turns fighters into stars. However, his back-to-back losses to the division's former champ have pushed "Suga" to the back of the contender line. But he has found new momentum in recent fights.

He was in a must-win situation at UFC 324 if he ever wanted to fight for gold again. In a hard-fought bout, he got a big W against top-10 fighter Yadong Song. O'Malley then followed it up with a TKO win over a surging Aiemann Zahabi at UFC Freedom 250. The win may have earned him a title shot in his next bout.

Merab Dvalishvili truly is "The Machine." His relentlessness and wrestling have turned him into one of the greatest bantamweights of all time. If there were any doubters after his 2024 win over Sean O'Malley, he silenced them with a decisive rematch victory, as well as two other title defenses.

However, staying at the top is always tough, and his title reign came to a definitive end at UFC 323 at the hands of Petr Yan. While he is no longer the champ, his place in division history is set.

Three straight losses had many wondering if Petr Yan's days as a top-five bantamweight were over. However, his recent wins over Yadon Song, Deiveson Figueiredo, and Marcus McGhee helped rebuild his title contender status. Earning a title shot at UFC 323.

In a rematch with a man who defeated him two years ago, the Russian was the greatest version of himself as he decisively defeated Merab Dvalishvili to become a two-time bantamweight champion. "No Mercy" proved he is completely back to being an elite fighter in the world.

title: Phillies World Series Champion Larry Christenson Dies at 72 During Family Fishing Trip
description: “The club and its fans are forever grateful for his contributions and the legacy he leaves behind in Philadelphia,” the Phillies wrote on social media
fullText:
Larry Christenson has died at age 72

The baseball star died while on a fishing trip with his family and friends in Washington state

Christenson was selected by the Phillies in the third round of the 1972 MLB Draft, after which he became a member of the 1980 World Series championship team and the National League pennant-winning club in 1983

Larry Christenson, a World Series champion with the Philadelphia Phillies, has died. He was 72.

The Philadelphia Phillies announced in an X post that the former pitcher died unexpectedly during a fishing trip with family and friends in Washington state on Friday, Aug. 28. No additional details about the circumstances of his death were immediately shared.

After being selected by the Philadelphia team in the third round of the 1972 MLB Draft, the Washington native made his big league debut on April 13, 1973, against the New York Mets at the age of 19. During his debut, Christenson earned the win in a complete game effort.

According to the MLB, Christenson remains the last pitcher to ever earn a complete game victory as a teenager in his MLB debut.

Throughout his 11 years with the Phillies, the pitcher became a member of the 1980 World Series championship team and the National League pennant-winning club in 1983. The Phillies also reached the playoffs six times in his 11 seasons.

"In addition to his legacy as a Phillies player, 'LC' was an active supporter of Phillies Charities and other local non-profits," the Phillies wrote on X. "The club and its fans are forever grateful for his contributions and the legacy he leaves behind in Philadelphia."

"We extend our heartfelt condolences to Larry's beloved daughters, Claire and Libby, his extended family and friends, and former teammates at this difficult time," the team added.

Christenson ranks ninth among all Phillies pitchers in career starts, per MLB. His 11 career home runs are also tied with Rick Wise for the most by a pitcher in franchise history.

Following the athlete's death, Larry Bowa, who played with Christenson from 1973 to 1981, shared an emotional tribute on social media.

"My heart is heavy today," he wrote. "LC was a tremendous teammate, an outstanding pitcher and a true friend."

"He was always the life of the clubhouse," he continued. "He will be deeply missed. My thoughts and prayers are with his family."

Former Phillies infielder Mike Schmidt also told ESPN that Christenson would be remembered as someone who was "very special, the guy that kept in touch with all of us."

"He always had a smile on his face, he never forgot a moment he spent with you," he said. "His passing will leave a hole in all of our hearts. May he rest in peace."

title: Three-week international break a concern - Mourinho
description: Jose Mourinho says the three-week international break is a “concern” for Real Madrid, with several key players facing a demanding schedule after the World Cup.
fullText:
Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho has raised concerns about the impact of September's three-week international break, highlighting the amount of time his players will be away from their club.

"The international break does concern me," Mourinho said. "It's a lot of time."

Speaking before Sunday's home La Liga match against Malaga (16:00 BST), Mourinho said he was mostly troubled by players linking up with their nations who then do not get game time.

"Players who will join their national teams to play don't worry me as much. It's the ones who join the national teams and are not really involved that concern me," he said.

"We'll see how we can go about this and work with the rest of the players. But not having players at my disposal for three weeks is a difficult situation."

The first international break of the 2026-27 men's football season next month will last a week longer than usual, with the traditional October break now scrapped.

In recent years, Fifa has used five primary international breaks during the season, in March, June, September, October and November.

But instead of separate breaks in September and October, there will now be a three-week gap for international fixtures across late September and early October, when countries will play four international matches instead of two. The existing international breaks in November, March and June will remain.

A number of reasons are behind the change, including the 2026 World Cup final being played on 19 July, the latest date for a summer World Cup since 1966. Player welfare and travel considerations were also taken into account when the changes were made.

"I totally respect the players' decisions and I don't want to dramatise too much, but very often they pick up injuries during those breaks and right after returning from an international break," Mourinho explained.

"So it does worry me, but this is the way these things are and we can't do much about it."

The Portuguese has already spoken at length about the World Cup players in his Real Madrid squad, including Jude Bellingham, Marc Cucurella and Kylian Mbappe, who have had a demanding summer.

He said the club are working to manage their workload to reduce the risk of injury.

In his pre-match media conference, Mourinho was also full of praise for Bellingham, highlighting his importance to the team beyond his attacking contributions.

"He is a unique kind of player, extremely important for the team," said Mourinho.

"His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front.

"We like talking about Kylian, Vini [Vinicius Jr] and Jude, but I'm really happy with all the players.

"We have great, great players here."

Mourinho also gave his perspective on the Ballon d'Or debate, arguing that winning the Champions League or World Cup should not automatically make a player the favourite for the individual award.

"It's a very beautiful thing individually and that enters into the individual history of a certain player," Mourinho said.

"I think it's normal that there are a dozen players of a very high level, of which we have three or four. It is normal that it exists as an ambition."

Mourinho suggested the prize should be ultimately measured by a player's lasting impact on the game.

"For me, the Ballon d'Or has to be one of those players that when he finishes playing, we miss for eternity," Mourinho said.

"I miss Maradona, Ronaldinho, Ronaldo, Cristiano, Messi, Zizou, Lothar Matthaus - I miss these people.

"You can't give the Ballon d'Or to a player because he won the Champions League or because he won the World Cup. It doesn't have to be from Paris St-Germain or the Spanish national team."
