title: Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining EU
description: Turbulent international affairs have brought the vote forward, but the campaign has focused more on Iceland's vital fishing industry.
fullText:
Icelanders are voting in a referendum to decide whether to resume talks on joining the European Union, 13 years after they were broken off.

In an indication of how tight the result is expected to be, the latest opinion poll put the No campaign in the lead with 51.6%. An earlier poll had put the Yes campaign ahead.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government had already intended to hold a referendum, but turbulent international affairs prompted her to bring it forward.

But the debate was fought less over Nato member Iceland's security concerns than over its vital fishing industry and sovereignty.

Iceland has a population of under 400,000. More than one in five voters had already cast their ballots in early voting before Saturday, according to Iceland's public broadcaster RUV.

The question on the ballot is: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

Although Iceland is already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone as part of the European Economic Area, EU membership would bring it into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland's application to join the EU was already well advanced when it put talks on hold in 2013, and European Commission officials have indicated that talks could be finalised in one or two years. Of the 35 so-called chapters of talks ranging from fisheries and economic policy to freedom of speech and free movement of goods, 27 had begun and 11 of them were provisionally complete.

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU. It would mean backing a move towards an accession agreement. Any deal would then have to be approved by a second referendum, as well by parliament, and the constitution would have to be amended. The EU's 27 member states would also have to sign it off.

One Yes-campaign group, "Yes to See", says Icelanders should at least see what deal they can get, so they have all the information before a final decision.

Equally, a No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.

Sovereignty has been a crucial issue in the pre-referendum debate. Iceland fought hard to become fully independent from Denmark in 1944, and its fishing and marine industries make up almost 40% of exports.

The No campaign fears losing control over Iceland's prized fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and has vowed never to share the country's waters with anyone. Brussels has indicated Iceland could earn some kind of exemption, but it is considered potentially the biggest obstacle to any agreement.

Many Icelanders remember the so-called Cod Wars with the UK that Iceland won in the 1970s. And fisheries was always the issue that stopped Iceland joining the EU before.

However, in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system, Reykjavik moved to start accession talks in 2009, only to bring them to a halt in 2013.

Iceland is now one of Europe's most affluent nations and Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC that "many people attribute this to Iceland's independence".

One Icelandic trade union survey suggested this year that the country was the most expensive in the world, far pricier than its Nordic neighbours.

Although it has the fifth highest GDP (economic output) per capita in the world, interest rates are stubbornly high at 8% and inflation has climbed to 5.6%.

Yes campaigners argue that the economic benefits of the EU would help bring the rates down.

Iceland may be a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

A bilateral US defence agreement has been in place since 1951 and the No campaign has said Iceland's security rests on both Nato and the US, and that EU membership is not a substitute for Nato.

Iceland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have viewed Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island with alarm.

However, there has also been concern at US President Donald Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland - especially the fact that he has confused it with Iceland.

This year the EU and Iceland signed a security and defence partnership, and EU officials said the EU "offers an anchor in a community of values, prosperity and security".

Ahead of the referendum, the two sides held a televised debate where the Yes campaign team was headed by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir and the No campaign was led by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, chair of the opposition Independence Party.

Kristrún told the audience that Iceland was already well integrated in the European Union, and becoming a member would be "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take".

She also made clear that a Yes vote did not necessarily mean that Iceland would join, and that if there was a No vote, the result would be respected.

Guðrún, meanwhile, stressed that the vote was not about whether Iceland should work well with Europe: "We already do, and we want that to continue."

Instead, she portrayed the referendum as a vote on whether Icelanders wanted to hand "decision-making powers" to Brussels on fisheries, agriculture and their natural resources.

Although geopolitics kick-started the government's decision to push for a return to EU talks, there has been little discussion of it during the campaign.

"It's lower on the agenda than many would think," says Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

title: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver
description: How to give a coding agent a real world, real demand, a protected measure, and enough memory to improve a complex feature.
fullText:
The first agent loops we built were barely loops: give the agent a plan, let it work until the tests pass, and return failures. That works when the tests describe the job. It fails when the job is to grow a product capability that we do not understand yet.

The agent keeps moving, but movement is not the problem. The tests only protect what we already know, and the important failures sit outside them. A screen can look complete while it stores nothing. An agent can give the right answer for the wrong reason. A scorer can reward behavior no user wants. More turns make each of those failures cheaper and faster.

In The Convergence Problem I argued that agents can own turns while people own rounds. I did not describe what the agent needs between those boundaries. It needs a harness that does three things. The harness must expose a real failure, locate the missing capability, and preserve the lesson after the session ends. That is a different machine from an agent with a retry prompt.

The obvious system is the feature. The less obvious one is the process that decides what the agent should change next. We have to engineer both.

The development agent changes the feature. The driver approaches the feature through the same surface a user would. The scorer reads what happened. The controller then chooses the next gap from that evidence. Repository state carries the decision into the next session.

An agent product usually puts another agent inside the feature. The two agents must remain separate. The development agent knows the code and the expected result. The product agent gets a fresh conversation and only the tools that the product exposes.

If they share context, the test is worthless. The product agent can succeed with knowledge that a user will never provide. The same harness works without a product agent. The driver can use a browser, API, command, or hardware simulator.

The prompt gets most of the attention because it is easy to see. The loop depends more on the world around it. First, the harness needs a reproducible starting point. The data, services, model, environment, and served code must match the recorded run. A reset should return the system to that point. A preflight should prove that it did.

If the world is unhealthy, the harness records no score. Infrastructure trouble is not evidence that the feature failed. This distinction prevents a large class of false repairs. Missing data can look like weak reasoning. Stale code can look like a broken contract.

Next, the harness needs real demand. We use a small corpus of requests that a person wrote or approved. The driver sends one request unchanged through a fresh interaction. It records the answer, tool calls, rejected actions, visible result, and persistent effects.

The effects matter most. Software can describe the correct action without performing it. It can render a plausible screen without changing the system beneath it. The prompt is therefore only one input to the run. The fixture, code revision, model, contract, and scorer belong beside it. A score without those inputs is only a number.

Every loop needs a deterministic floor. Tests, validators, schemas, and effect checks hold behavior that the feature already earned. The floor starts green. If it turns red, that regression becomes the next job. The floor cannot tell us what to build next. For that, we drive a real request and inspect the shortfall.

Some shortfalls support a mechanical score. Others need a screenshot, repeated samples, or a person who understands the work. Those signals can be noisy. One perfect run proves that success is possible. It says little about whether success is reliable.

The signals choose a direction, while the floor preserves prior progress. That separation keeps the loop honest. A new capability can move the product forward without erasing the path behind it.

Once the world and measures exist, the round itself is simple.

One gap does not mean one file. It means one causal claim. The missing capability may cross the data model, tool contract, runtime, agent instruction, interface, and effect check. The round should close that whole path.

Partial paths create the most convincing failures. The interface exists, but nothing produces its data. The tool returns success, but the state does not change. A narrow path that works from request to effect is worth more than five layers of unfinished possibility.

The classification step prevents random repairs. A symptom can belong to the world, domain, contract, runtime, steering, surface, or harness. Without that step, every agent failure becomes a prompt problem. Every visual failure becomes a frontend problem. The loop changes the nearest thing instead of the right thing.

Changing one causal gap also makes the result attributable. If a round changes five independent levers, nobody knows which lesson to preserve.

An autonomous loop will optimize whatever measure it can reach, including a bad one. The harness therefore needs an authority model. Ours has three levels.

Free files are normal implementation levers. The loop can change and measure them inside the assigned scope. Propose files cross a boundary. The loop can record evidence and suggest a change, but a person decides. Frozen files define the exam. They include the approved corpus, fixture, existing rungs, score rules, and judgment rubric.

The loop can add a regression check for a failure it observed. It cannot weaken an existing check or lower the threshold. It also cannot change a product lever and the measure of that lever in the same round. Otherwise, it grades its own repair.

Learned judges need the same protection. A visual judge remains evidence until its rankings agree with repeated human rankings. This limits the loop’s authority, but it makes the result credible.

Every product round also tests the harness. The driver can hide a failure. The fixture can omit a necessary case. The scorer can punish correct behavior. The procedure can waste the same hour twice.

We end each round with one question:

What cost time that a rule or check could prevent?

The first occurrence becomes evidence. Repeated friction can change the driver, facts, or standing procedure. Self-improvement happens when the loop promotes a specific failure into a durable constraint. It does not rewrite its operating system after every surprise. Sometimes the right change is subtraction. A false warning or misleading rung teaches the loop to avoid good behavior.

There are really three loops running at different speeds. The product loop closes one capability each round. The harness loop changes when repeated evidence exposes a development failure. The direction loop sits outside both. A person reads a batch of evidence and decides whether to continue, redirect, or stop.

Keeping those loops separate matters. The development agent can propose a new direction. It cannot decide that its own result is good enough.

None of this can live only in the current conversation. Agent sessions end, context compresses, and the next session starts without the old reasoning. We keep a small package under goals/:

LOOP.md changes when the process changes. STATE.md changes after each round. The distinction makes sessions disposable without making the work forgetful. A new agent reads the goal, procedure, state, and evidence, then continues from the same decision.

This is more than context preservation. The files make the development process inspectable. We can see why the loop chose a gap, which evidence supported the change, and whether the next run improved the same request.

We run the inner loop in small batches. Three rounds usually produce enough evidence for a decision without giving the system room to drift. At the boundary, a person chooses whether to continue the queue, redirect the next batch, or stop. The loop stops sooner when it cannot reproduce or attribute a failure. It also stops when the world is unhealthy or the repair needs a frozen change.

This is the human-owned round from the convergence post. The agent owns the turns inside it. The boundary exists because the score cannot decide the product’s direction.

Most tickets do not need any of this. If complete tests describe the work, give the agent the tests and let it finish. The harness earns its cost when use must reveal the capability sequence. The system must also expose effects that the harness can observe.

Start with three requests, one fixture, one score command, one loop file, one state file, and a three-round budget. Add a new control only after a failure justifies it.

The quality of an agent loop is not how long it runs or how many commits it produces. It is what remains after a round. A good round leaves a working capability, evidence that it works, and a harness that will not pay for the same lesson twice. That is an agent loop worth leaving alone with a complex feature.

title: Pritchard retains rowing world title in Amsterdam
description: Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard retains his PR1 men's single sculls world title at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam.
fullText:
Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard retained his PR1 men's single sculls world title at the Rowing World Championships in Amsterdam.

Pritchard, from Mumbles near Swansea, crossed the line in eight minutes and 50.46 seconds to set a new record at the World Championships.

The 34-year-old finished just shy of the eight minutes and 40.38 seconds world record time he set at the 2025 European Championships in Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

After a strong start, Italian Giacomo Perini and Australian Erik Horrie closed the gap on Pritchard towards the 500m mark before the Welshman stretched his lead, eventually winning by 6.81 seconds.

Pritchard named BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year 2025

Pritchard is one of para-rowing's leading forces. Since winning Paralympic gold in 2024, he has set multiple world records and added European and world titles to his list of accolades.

The 2025 BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year award winner and his rivals had to deal with adversity during the championships in the Netherlands, with their semi-final delayed due to thunderstorms, reducing recovery windows.

Pritchard's second world championship win came weeks after claiming the 2026 European title in Varese, Italy, and having suffered an injury earlier this month.

After retaining his global title, Pritchard told World Rowing it had been a "story of calamities" following Friday's thunderstorms and the issues he faced in the race.

He also noted his rivals are "getting faster off the first 500".

Pritchard added: "But you've just got to try and back yourself, back all the training that you do.

"We're in some lovely Welsh weather at the moment, some liquid sunshine, so it's great that all the training that I do on the (river) Tawe back home."

title: Itauma v Hrgovic - heavyweight world title fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight world title fight between Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic.
fullText:
Britain could have a new heavyweight world champion on Saturday when Moses Itauma faces Croatian Filip Hrgovic at London's O2 Arena for the vacant IBF title.

The 21-year-old Briton has won all 14 of his professional fights, 12 by stoppage, and has established himself as one of the division's most exciting young prospects.

A victory would make the Chatham fighter the youngest heavyweight world champion since Mike Tyson in 1986.

But Hrgovic is a major step up. The experienced 34-year-old - a 2016 Olympic bronze medallist - has a record of 20 wins and one defeat, with 15 victories inside the distance.

You can follow radio commentary from 21:00 BST on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, before switching to BBC Radio 5 Live from 22:00.

Live text commentary will begin at 19:30 on the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for the bout.

"Hrgovic right now is possibly the best fighter for him to face. On paper it's a test but I don't think it will be a test. I don't think Moses will be under any form of pressure in a fight like this.

"I think it's going to be one of Moses' easiest nights of his career and he'll win a world title."

"I do have Itauma as the favourite. He is no doubt a better fighter but still unproven over the long distance. And think people are maybe just forgetting just how tough Hrgovic is and how good he is at taking a shot.

"I can see Itauma blowing him away early because he's so accurate but I can also see Hrgovic riding the storm and it becoming a more difficult fight in the second half for Itauma.

"But I still see Moses coming out on top. Hrgovic cuts a lot and I can see this being stopped on cuts because Itauma will hit him so often."

"It's a really good fight. It's a test that Itauma has been needing for a while. Stylistically, it's very interesting. I think this fight will be really hard or really easy. I don't see a middle ground where Itauma will cruise and will look great doing it.

"I think he either gets rid of him inside three rounds or this is the acid test we've all been waiting for.

"Hrgovic is brave and tough but he stands up tall and is quite easy to hit. Itauma has got the whole package. He's in and out of range, he's sharp. He's got the footwork and speed of a cruiserweight and the power of a heavyweight.

"So I'll go with Itauma inside three rounds."

"I've said for a while that I'd back Moses againt any heavyweight on the planet, other than Oleksandr Usyk. Going by Usyk's last performance against Rico Verhoeven, I'd probably back Moses against him too.

"Hrgovic is technically good and will ask Itauma a few more questions than previous opponents. But ultimately, I think the speed and timing of Moses will be the difference.

"He will get to him in the sixth or seventh round and stop him, with maybe a few knockdowns along the way."

"I favour Moses to get the win. I know Hrgovic will come prepared. He's game and not a pushover. He's coming to win a world title. So it won't be a straightforward fight, but it will be a good fight.

"I'm rooting for Moses so I say he will win by any means necessary. Whether it's points, stoppage or even a disqualification."

"I fancy Itauma to make a statement with a stoppage mid to late rounds. I think the cuts of Hrgovic may come into play, but I also think Itauma will take his time, find the gaps and then get the stoppage."

"Both men can punch hard - expect fireworks on Saturday. This is the acid test for Itauma. You have to favour the younger man because of his southpaw speed, skill, IQ and the foundations seem to be there for a huge career ahead.

"But Hrgovic has momentum and this is his chance for a world title and he will leave no stone unturned."

"I think it's Itauma's time and he stops him. I think he will be too much for a 34-year-old Hrgovic, who has never really pushed on like we expected him to.

"It could be with sharp punches and he knocks Hrgovic out within four or five rounds, or he stops him on cuts a little bit later on. Hrgovic's skin really shreds and that's the danger with Itauma's punches. His timing and accuracy is really good.

"Hrgovic is very tough, but he can be one dimensional in terms of his feet coming forward. He's a bit cumbersome and he leans back and is there to be hit.

"I think Itauma will close the distance really well going forward or dropping back with great devastating counter-punches as he's retreating."

"As this fight gets closer - and this always happens with big fights - opinions change. My opinion hasn't changed but it has definitely got tighter.

"I still think Itauma will get this done but I'm not as convinced as I was three or four months ago. Hrgovic looks in incredible shape. He's been training away in the mountains of Big Bear Lake in California with Abel Sanchez.

"I do think Itauma gets it done between rounds six and eight and it's a stoppage on cuts, but not without facing some trouble first."

"This is, on paper, a test for Itauma. Hrgovic is big, strong and his resume is far stronger.

"But still, are we allowed to dream about a young heavyweight who could change the landscape? I think we should.

"Itauma has the speed, agility, and the thought process of his work is what sets him apart from other heavyweights right now.

"I really strongly believe he will do a job on Saturday. I think he will be impressive and wear down a really robust and physically tough Hrgovic.

"I think Itauma wins within six rounds."

description: France's Cassandre Beaugrand earns her fourth straight win in the World Triathlon Championship Series as Britain's Beth Potter comes second in Weihai.
fullText:
France's Cassandre Beaugrand earned her fourth straight win in the World Triathlon Championship Series as Britain's Beth Potter came second in Weihai.

Olympic champion Beaugrand surged away in the final kilometre of the 10km run to finish in one minute 49.20 seconds and maintain her perfect record in this season's Championship Series.

Beaugrand's victory in China followed a thrilling tussle up until the final stretch, as Olympic bronze medalist Potter finished six seconds behind the 29-year-old.

Germany's Lisa Tertsch was third, a further 18 seconds back.

"This one was definitely not easy," said Beaugrand.

"I was feeling great on the swim, great on the bike. The run was quite hard with Beth pushing the pace. I just tried my best to keep up and trust my finish."

Beaugrand exited the two-lap 1500m swim in third behind Britain's Tilly Anema and Brazil's Vittoria Lopez.

After a close bike section, where a pack of more than 30 cyclists merged together at the front, Beaugrand, Potter and Tertsch started to break away on foot.

On the final lap as Tertsch started to fade away, Potter fought valiantly but she could not keep in touch with Beaugrand's searing pace.

Beaugrand's victory means she has overtaken Potter, despite competing in fewer races this year, to go top of the World Triathlon Championship Series standings.

The men's race was won by Switzerland's Max Studer, who finished in 1:41:08.

Spain's David Cantero del Campo finished 10 seconds behind, with Canada's Tyler Mislawchuk in third, a further seven seconds back.

There is one more regular-season event in the Czech Republic on 13 September, before the Grand Final in Spain on 23 September.

fullText:
In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding

It’s a bleak moment for young people entering the workforce for the first time. For decades, a university degree seemed to promise a stable career – but entry-level white-collar jobs across almost all sectors are being disrupted by AI. Budding accountants, software engineers and junior lawyers increasingly find themselves displaced by cheap automation.

Even creative fields are struggling against AI tech that can produce artwork, lengthy prose or complex design briefs in seconds.

But many young workers have responded by turning to what they see as “AI-proof” heritage crafts. These are the centuries-old, hands-on jobs, such as boat-making, metalwork or bookbinding, that require specialist knowledge built on creative judgment and dexterity, skills not yet mastered by AI.

Eryn Lawley, a 27-year-old politics graduate, said future-proofing her career meant walking away from the digital world. She is now a second-year bookbinder apprentice at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire, learning a trade whose core techniques have not changed for centuries.

“Even just staring at a screen too long was bad for me,” she said. “I always wanted to do something more material, and I think there is something more inherently valuable to something when it is made by a person.”

The work at Ludlow is slow, detailed and tactile. The bookbinding process is almost entirely by hand, using Victorian-built presses, foil-blocking machines and glue brushes.

“People are discovering that, as everything is already decided for you by a computer or algorithm, being able to make or own something physically is good,”

Lawley said. “And it is very satisfying to repeat a task to perfection. It is meditative as a job so it is extremely low-cortisol.”

Paul Kidson, Ludlow chief executive and a fourth-generation bookbinder, said an influx of interest from young people represented a lifeline for a rapidly shrinking industry. He estimates there are now fewer than 50 handcraft-operating bookbinders in Britain today.

“British bookbinding has a terrific reputation across the world, but like so many things in the 50s, 60s and 70s, the training just started to dry up,” Kidson said. “All the formal apprentice schemes collapsed in the early 1980s, and the industry got no training at all.

“We have to train our own people because you can’t recruit at volume because there aren’t any [courses]. Fortunately there is now a desire among a lot of people to want to have the satisfaction of actually making something.”

There is no lack of commercial demand. High-end publishers are betting that shoppers will pay a premium for objects that are crafted by human hands. Joanna Reynolds, chief executive of the Folio Society book publisher – which partnered with Ludlow for a limited edition release of a Game of Thrones book – said the company rejected generative AI tools in its creative processes.

“We do not use AI in terms of our art,” she said. “We believe in the importance of supporting the creative world, and we know there is huge pressure on them at the moment. Their skills and their abilities need to be supported by as many people as possible.”

The number of young people hoping to fill these creative posts is growing rapidly. Cox London, a design house that specialises in artistic metalwork, started its apprenticeship scheme last year. Nicola Cox, a co-founder, said this year the company received more than 160 applications for two apprenticeship places.

“People want to make things and work with materials, [to] have that closeness with it,” she said. “There is AI-proofness about art that is made with someone’s hands. There is a real resonance in something that has a mark and the energy of human hands.”

For Lucky Emerson, an apprentice at Cox London, there is a “worrying feeling” that AI is taking over the creative world.

“The physicality of actually making things is incomparable, especially when people crave originality. Even though technology has advanced, handcrafted art is considered a lot more valuable and will always remain that way.”

Nazifa Tabassum, also an apprentice at Cox London, said she did not think AI would replace her work, but that it could change it.

“For me it isn’t just about making things with my hands,” she said. “It’s about continuously developing my skills, and using technology where it adds value, while still providing the expertise and craftsmanship that people can’t easily automate.

“I see AI as a tool that can assist, but not something that replaces, the satisfaction and value of skilled manual, handcrafted work.”At the National Theatre in London, technical apprenticeships span everything from IT to traditional wig-making, costume design, prop-making and metalwork.

“Our apprenticeships are partly about the need to create a more representative workforce, both for the National Theatre and for the [wider] creative sector,” said Kath Geraghty, head of technical qualifications.

“It is also about plugging the skill gap. These theatre crafts are dying out – our metalworkers are all over 50, wig-making as a skill is really dying. There’s a real need to create our own talent.

“And it’s always been about creating a skilled workforce for the wider creative sector beyond theatre, such as film, TV and broadcast.”

Sarah Ray-Dobson, a 27-year-old apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre, said she felt her practice had been shielded from AI disruption that affected other creative pursuits.

“Everything I’ve been doing for the past two years is very hands-on,” she said. “At my level, it has not been affected by AI.”

But Geraghty adds that, like many employers, the National Theatre is struggling with the huge number of AI-generated applications for its apprenticeship programme.

“We used to think that 100 applicants was a popular apprenticeship,” she said. “In this most recent round of recruitment, we had 728 applications for one role.

“We haven’t yet worked out how to manage it, because it’s not viable for our staff to read 700 applications with care and attention. But the job market that young people are in is difficult, and they are applying for anything they can.”

fullText:
Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’

The game that graced us with Bathtub Geralt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)

As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”

The elephant in the room, though, is that The Witcher 3’s 2016 expansion Blood and Wine felt like a natural conclusion to Geralt’s tale. After decades covered in entrails, the legendary monster slayer hangs up his dual swords for a well-earned life of luxury on his recently acquired vineyard estate. What can he possibly have left to do?

“That is certainly something we thought through,” says Blacha. “Geralt retired in Toussaint – but then his best friend comes calling. I don’t think many of us would turn down that request.”

So, foppish fan favourite Dandelion the bard pulls the witcher back into action, asking Geralt to come to his aid in his homeland of Letten. It’s a seemingly idyllic land of bountiful harvests and rowdy festivals that hides some sinister secrets.

It’s been exciting, and nostalgic. We spent so long with Geralt, but have also learned a lot in the 10-plus years we’ve been away from him,” says Blacha. “With Songs of the Past, we really wanted to return to The Witcher’s roots. That meant drawing on old beliefs and folklore, revisiting landscapes inspired by Poland’s history and countryside, and staying true to the series’ tradition of difficult dilemmas. Going back to all of this has been a pleasure.”

The team has also put to bed rumours that this expansion will be a prequel to The Witcher 4. Songs of the Past is focused on the gruff, grey witcher we’ve already come to love, not Ciri, the younger protagonist of the forthcoming title. Rather, the expansion has all the trappings that seasoned Witcher fans should recognise, with a morally murky narrative brought to life by returning voice actors Doug Cockle and John Schwab, who reprise their roles as Geralt and Dandelion.

There are a few new features to play around with, though: CD Projekt has enhanced Geralt’s combat and skill trees, and he now wields a chain weapon alongside his steel and silver swords. There are also new DNA-modifying mutagens to play around with, tweaking Geralt’s biology and, therefore, his supernatural skills.

The Witcher 3 is a modern classic that has already come to a gratifying end: bringing Geralt out of retirement is a risky move. But when his medallion starts humming, the White Wolf is still ready to answer the call.

fullText:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

Experts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in women

Doctors have discovered a way to use routine mammograms that screen for breast cancer to spot heart disease, the world’s leading – and frequently underdiagnosed – cause of death in women.

Researchers analysed the scans using artificial intelligence and were able to successfully identify women with coronary heart disease, high blood pressure or who had suffered a stroke.

Experts said it meant breast screening for cancer could become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with heart disease, and other cardiovascular issues, as well as spotting breast cancer early.

Millions of women are living with undetected heart disease. For decades, it has often been misdiagnosed or not picked up until the late stages of the disease.

Details of the breakthrough were presented in Munich at the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress, the world’s largest heart conference. The implications are significant because hundreds of millions of women undergo mammograms every year.

Doctors in Israel examined 97,364 scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54. By cross-referencing medical records, they found 16% of the women had high blood pressure, 2.5% had coronary heart disease, and 2.5% had experienced a stroke.

A machine-learning model was trained to identify women with these conditions and was able to reliably identify women who had suffered a stroke, based upon their mammogram alone, 86% of the time.

For high blood pressure and coronary heart disease, it was 79% and 78% reliable at distinguishing between the women with the condition and those without. The results were also consistent regardless of age, or whether or not a woman also had cancer.

Dr Viana Copeland from Tel Aviv University, Israel, presented the findings to delegates in Munich. “Despite being the leading cause of death in women worldwide, CVD [cardiovascular disease] is consistently underdiagnosed and undertreated,” she said.

“A common finding in our medical centre, and around the world, is that when women do seek medical help, their CVD is already advanced. On the other hand, many women do attend routine breast cancer screening, even when they haven’t sought care for cardiovascular symptoms.”

Because mammography is already widely used, analysing breast scans for information about a woman’s heart health “could potentially offer a scalable approach without requiring an additional imaging examination,” Copeland added.

“Mammography also reaches many women in midlife, an important period for recognising and addressing cardiovascular risk.”

A team of doctors and medical researchers are working to improve the accuracy of the AI model and reduce false results, while increasing the number of heart conditions it can detect.

Elena Arbelo, an expert member of the European Society of Cardiology communication committee, said the findings were “compelling”.

“A mammogram may one day do more than look for breast cancer – it may also offer a window on to cardiovascular health. That matters because CVD in women is still too often recognised late.”

She added: “The challenge now is to establish accuracy and reliability – to move from experimentation to clinical implementation.”

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation, a charity, also welcomed the breakthrough.

She said: “Heart disease is the world’s biggest killer of not only men, but also women. Despite this, the myth persists that it’s only a ‘man’s disease’, meaning that when it comes to the heart, women are disproportionally unaware, unheard, underdiagnosed, undertreated and typically underrepresented in clinical research.

“It is exciting to think that if the approach used in this large study from Israel is further proven, it could lead to better and earlier cardiovascular disease detection and prevention for women. AI could one day allow breast cancer screening programmes to become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with the highest risk of dangerous cardiovascular disease, as well as spotting breast cancer early.”

title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
description: King Oyo ascended to the throne of Uganda's Tooro kingdom when he was just three years old.
fullText:
A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.

Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.

The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.

Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.

Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.

"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."

The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.

Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".

"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.

When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.

The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.

The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.

Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.

Others have also paid their respects to the late king.

The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.

Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".

The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".

Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.

Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"

Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

WASHINGTON, Aug 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration has issued a memo for universities that seeks to restrict issuance of certain internship work ‌authorizations for international students as the federal government warned that colleges not complying with the regulations may lose certification ‌to enroll foreign students.

The federal memo dated August 24 said the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which is part of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ​agency, has "observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that appear to violate regulatory requirements which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum."

"Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enroll foreign students," the memo said.

It resulted in some schools, including the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of California, Berkeley, pausing certain ‌applications for work authorizations for international students.

"UCLA ⁠has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorizations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines next steps," a UCLA spokesperson said.

UC Berkeley's international office said the August 24 memo was "more narrow in focus, more ⁠direct, and includes content that is more restrictive in nature." The federal government had also issued an earlier memo in mid-August.

UC Berkeley's international office said it is unlikely that it will process certain work authorization applications "in the near future" and urged those international students to plan ​accordingly.

It said ​it will continue processing "degree-requirement" CPT as normal and would resume processing "Doctoral ​Dissertation and Master's Thesis Research CPT." The office said ‌it would consult legal experts to develop new processes aligning with new federal requirements.

"Nothing about these regulations has changed," the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent, said in a statement. "However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated."

Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding threats over issues like pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, climate programs and transgender policies. Rights advocates have raised free speech, academic freedom ‌and due process concerns.

Separately, the U.S. Justice Department alleged on Thursday admissions ​practices at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Services favored ​Black and Hispanic applicants, citing findings of a probe ​as the Trump administration continued its diversity crackdown.

"We are disappointed by the DOJ's conclusions, which we believe ‌are incorrect," the university said, saying the admissions policies ​were in compliance with law and ​not discriminatory.

The Justice Department has alleged similar bias at other schools, saying the department aims for settlement talks. If those efforts fail, the department will file suit, it said.

Trump's administration has also revoked visas of student protesters over pro-Palestinian ​protests that it casts as antisemitic and ‌sympathetic to extremists.

Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposition to Israel's assault on Gaza and its occupation of ​Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights is not the same as supporting extremism.

title: Will fast-tracked Itauma become world champion at 21?
description: Can heavyweight Moses Itauma become world champion at 21 by beating Filip Hrgovic on Saturday or has the fast-tracked Briton arrived too soon?
fullText:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma pulls out his phone and scrolls through his pictures.

He shows a meme featuring former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo in traditional attire, standing with his hands on his hips and staring deadpan into the camera.

"This is how an African dad looks at you when you pursue a career that goes against his wishes and you turn out to be successful," a chuckling Itauma reads aloud to BBC Sport. "That is pretty much my dad."

Itauma was born in Slovakia to a Nigerian father and a Slovak mother before moving to Kent as a young child.

His parents originally wanted him to become a doctor or a lawyer. But once his older brother turned professional and the family recognised Itauma's exceptional natural talent, their stance softened.

"Don't worry about school. Just focus on your boxing," his mother eventually said.

That decision has paid off spectacularly.

At 21, Itauma steps into the ring against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday for the vacant IBF title with the chance to become the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history.

"There's a lot of expectations on my shoulders to carry the flag of British boxing. I just have to live up to it," Itauma says.

Victory against Croatia's Hrgovic would put Itauma on the path to becoming the next big name in British heavyweight boxing, with Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua inching closer to the end of their storied careers.

Fury, with his Netflix documentaries and larger-than-life personality, has always made himself the attraction. Itauma is more like Joshua - guarded and keeping the media at arm's length.

"What irritates me most is when people think you're public property," he says.

"What people don't know about me is that I don't actually want to be in the limelight. The way my career is going, I just have no choice."

Like Joshua, Itauma often appears uninterested in the theatrics of fight week. When Hrgovic interrupted during Thursday's news conference, Itauma calmly asked host Adam Smith for the next question.

There are similarities in their careers, too.

Joshua fought Charles Martin for the IBF title in his 16th pro bout, having boxed 34 rounds. Itauma arrives at his first world-title opportunity a fight sooner and with 31 rounds logged.

While Joshua had an Olympic gold medal and a deeper amateur background, victory for Itauma would make comparisons unavoidable - eclipsing Joshua to become the fastest British heavyweight to win a world title.

Itauma's trainer Ben Davison, who also worked with Joshua and Fury, believes he has the temperament to handle what comes next.

"Pressure is a privilege," he says.

"Moses has already had that pressure for such a long time and I just think it's water off a duck's back."

Boxing's best young prospects tend to be handled carefully and are given time to learn before dangerous tests arrive.

Itauma, however, has been fast-tracked to his world-title shot.

Francis Warren - son of Queensberry chief Frank - first noticed him as a teenager, sparring established professionals. Former British heavyweight champion Jeamie 'TKV' Tshikeva was there even earlier.

"Moses was a big 11 or 12-year-old, around 75 to 80kg, (11st 11lb to 12st 8lb) and sparred an adult of the same weight," TKV says. "He really showed up, put hands on this grown man, and I was shocked.

"The guy he sparred was around 25. Imagine going home and telling your wife you got beat up by a kid."

Itauma's progress has been marked by destructive stoppages over Dillian Whyte and Jermaine Franklin. They may not be world-beaters, but the manner of those wins strengthened belief Itauma was destined for the top.

When Oleksandr Usyk vacated the IBF title and Frank Sanchez agreed to step aside, Itauma's fight with Hrgovic was elevated into a world-title contest.

Suddenly, the fast track looked, to some, like a shortcut.

Hrgovic - even before the IBF belt was on the line - claimed Itauma had been handed "everything on a plate". On social media, there was a similar feeling - perhaps a final eliminator would have been a more natural way to earn his shot.

Itauma, though, has little interest in proving himself to the doubters.

"It's a lose-lose situation for me because if I win, I've done what people expect, and if I lose, it's just like, I wasn't as good as what I thought," he says.

"I don't find happiness in trying to please other people's expectations."

Mike Tyson's mark as the youngest heavyweight champion in history - 20 years, four months and 22 days - remains boxing's ultimate holy grail.

While that record has passed, victory over Hrgovic would make Itauma the second-youngest heavyweight champion ever and boxing's youngest active world champion.

The Chatham heavyweight has never fought 12 rounds. He has never even sparred 12.

"Although I haven't gone 12 rounds and I haven't taken one on the chin, I don't think that's a characteristic you need to become a heavyweight champion," he says.

But what happens when his power does not end the fight? What happens when an opponent is still standing in round eight, still dangerous, still coming back?

TKV, who has sparred Joshua, Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley, has seen enough behind closed doors to believe Itauma can handle it.

"Moses works hard even though he hasn't had to face adversity in his fights or training," he says. "I've never seen him slack. He's fast, sharp, a good learner and I rarely see him get hit.

"I believe he can do the rounds, too. He has the potential to dominate the division for years."

There is no doubt within Itauma's camp that he belongs at this level. But all the outside questions over timing, merit and readiness will fade when the first bell sounds.

On Saturday, the prodigy has 12 rounds - if he needs them - to write his own chapter in heavyweight history.

title: Simeone would welcome Alvarez back to training amid Barca row
description: Diego Simeone says he will do everything he can to make Julian Alvarez feel important at Atletico Madrid, after confirming the Argentina international will miss Saturday’s match against Sevilla.
fullText:
Diego Simeone says he will "do everything" he can to make Julian Alvarez "feel important" at Atletico Madrid when the forward returns to training, as uncertainty continues over his situation at the Spanish club.

It comes as Atletico Madrid made it clear that they would not sell him to Barcelona, with a move to Arsenal looking like the striker's only way out.

Simeone confirmed Alvarez will not travel with Atletico for Saturday's La Liga game at Sevilla saying he is not currently in good health, having missed his third consecutive training session on Friday.

"From the moment he returns to training, I will do everything I can to make him feel important," said Atletico manager Simeone.

Asked whether Alvarez's situation could still be reversed, Simeone added: "As long as you have your health, everything in life can be turned around."

This week the La Liga club released two public statements in the space of 24 hours reiterating their stance that Alvarez will not be granted his wish to join Barca in the coming days.

Simeone said he understood why questions about Alvarez would dominate his news conference but insisted the club had already been "forceful and clear" in explaining the situation.

"I'm still in the same position, hoping, from a sporting point of view, to be able to help him in the best way so that he continues to be the very important player he is for us," he said.

"Julian will not be there [on Saturday] against Sevilla, who have just won two games and will be high with confidence."

Injured Norwegian striker Alexander Sorloth is also unavailable, leaving Atletico without two attacking options.

"Sorloth's absence hurts us. He's very important for us," Simeone said.

"In this situation with Julian, it has much more impact. The team will try collectively to find solutions to score goals and win. We are working with them on that awareness. We are going to try to improve it collectively."

Simeone also rejected concerns that the uncertainty surrounding Alvarez could affect his squad.

"Honestly, no," he said. "The boys are working very well, especially the World Cup players. The team played good matches against Malaga and Villarreal and we are focused on playing a good match [against Sevilla]."

New defender Cristian Romero, who joined Atelti from Tottenham for 40m euros (£34.2m) this summer, will travel with the squad to Sevilla, although Simeone said: "He needs time to find his best form and we will not speed up the time to rush him, so that he feels that he is in a position to perform as well as he should."

title: Hrgovic slaps Itauma after being pushed off stage at weigh-in
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma pushes Filip Hrgovic off the stage before the Croat slaps him as chaos erupts at the weigh-in for Saturday's world-title bout.
fullText:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma pushed Filip Hrgovic off the stage before the Croat slapped him as chaos erupted at the weigh-in for Saturday's world-title bout.

The pair will fight for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at London's O2 Arena, with Itauma bidding to become the second-youngest heavyweight champion in history.

The 21-year-old had refused to engage with Hrgovic's attempts to rile him during fight week but was in a fierce mood as the pair exchanged expletives during a charged face-off.

As Hrgovic turned to pose for photographs, Itauma shoved him in the back, sending the 34-year-old off the stage.

Hrgovic climbed back up, reached through security and slapped the Chatham fighter in the face before members of both teams became involved as security separated them.

"He pushed me first so I just gave it back. He started it," Hrgovic said, before breaking off from the interview to stare down Itauma.

Will fast-tracked Itauma become world champion at 21?

I'll send Itauma back to high school - Hrgovic

Itauma 'million times better' than Fury and Joshua - Hamed

Earlier in the week, Itauma said Hrgovic - who has repeatedly labelled him a "kid" - was beginning to get under his skin.

"I don't know, I just lost it a little bit. I had a little itch and I had to scratch it," Itauma said.

Before the fracas, an in-shape Hrgovic had weighed in at his lightest in seven years - 16st 12lb (107kg), 12 pounds lighter than for his victory over Dave Allen in May.

Itauma, who would also become the second-youngest world champion from Britain if he wins, weighed 17st 4lb (110kg), the same as for his victory over Jermaine Franklin in March.

Friday's ceremonial weigh-in took place at London's Spitalfields Market, with the official weigh-in held behind closed doors earlier in the day.

Several hundred people gathered around the food stalls and coffee kiosks for the event, with Itauma walking through the crowd to loud cheers.

He was smiling as he made his way through the market, where some had come specifically for the weigh-in while others were simply passing through and stopped to see what the fuss was about.

Itauma has the unbeaten record, knockout power and reputation as one of boxing's brightest young talents, but is still building his profile outside the sport.

Sometimes, though, it is what happens outside the ring that gets people talking.

The incident did not appear premeditated, with Itauma looking irritated by what Hrgovic was saying before the shove.

"He wants to stamp his authority and I think that's what he was doing there - stamping his authority before he gets in the ring," promoter Frank Warren said.

"He's showing he's not fazed by what Filip brings with his experience and sterling amateur background. He's up for this, alight and on fire."

title: Inter Miami name Kily González head coach
description: Miami CF have named Cristian 'Kily' González as their new head coach, the club announced Thursday The 52-year-old former Argentine international officially replaces his ex-Alb...
fullText:
Inter Miami CF have named Cristian 'Kily' González as their new head coach, the club announced Thursday

The 52-year-old former Argentine international officially replaces his ex-Albiceleste teammate Javier Mascherano, who departed the club in April.

The Herons had been led by Guillermo Hoyos, who will remain charge of the team until the arrival of the new head coach and his coaching staff.

González joins Miami with a half-decade of coaching experience in his native Argentina, most recently with Club Atlético Platense during the 2025 Primera División season.

He began his first-team managerial career at boyhood club Rosario Central (2020-22) before taking the reins at Unión Santa Fe between 2023-25.

As a player, González starred for the likes of Rosario Central, Boca Juniors, Real Zaragoza, Valencia and Inter Milan. He represented Argentina at the 2002 FIFA World Cup and helped his country win gold at the 2004 Summer Olympic Games.

González takes over a Miami side led by Argentina legend Lionel Messi and an A-list supporting cast highlighted by fellow global superstars Luis Suárez, Rodrigo De Paul and Casemiro.

Since Messi's summer 2023 arrival, the Herons have won three titles: Leagues Cup 2023, the 2024 MLS Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup 2025 presented by Audi.

The first-ever back-to-back Landon Donovan MLS MVP (2024, '25), Messi has 14g/9a this season while also guiding Argentina, along with De Paul, to the 2026 World Cup final.

Miami are second in the Eastern Conference with 39 points. They're looking to become the first repeat MLS Cup champions since the LA Galaxy in 2011-12.

title: Ipswich sign Argentina World Cup winner Palacios
description: Argentina midfielder Exequiel Palacios becomes the first World Cup winner to sign for Ipswich Town after joining from Bayer Leverkusen.
fullText:
Argentina midfielder Exequiel Palacios has become the first World Cup winner to sign for Ipswich Town after joining from Bayer Leverkusen.

Palacios, 27, left the Bundesliga club for an undisclosed fee and has signed a four-year contract with the Premier League newcomers.

He was part of the Argentina side that both won the World Cup in 2022 and reached the final this summer while he also won the Copa America twice with his country.

"This is a club with great ambition and I am excited to play football in England and compete against some of the best clubs and players in the world," Palacios said.

Palacios, Ipswich's 11th signing of the transfer window, started Argentina's 3-1 win against World Cup debutants Jordan in the group stage in his only appearance at the 2026 tournament.

Ipswich manager Gary O'Neil added: "He is a player who has had real success at the top level of the game, winning the biggest prize of all in the World Cup, as well as major trophies at club level.

"That experience will be vital for us as we continue to work to improve the squad this summer."

Palacios made his senior debut for his boyhood club River Plate in 2015 and won the Copa Libertadores in 2018 and the Copa Argentina twice.

He moved to Germany in 2020 and made 24 appearances as Leverkusen claimed their first-ever Bundesliga title in 2023-24.

Under current Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso, he also won the DFB Pokal and the German Super Cup during his six years at the BayArena.

He departs Leverkusen after making 186 appearances and scoring 15 goals.

Ipswich have spent more than £150m since returning to the Premier League and are also progressing with a move to sign Tammy Abraham on loan from Aston Villa.

They made a winning return to the top flight, defeating Sunderland 2-1 at Portman Road and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup at the expense of League One Leicester City.
